strengths: Addresses a relevant bottleneck in visual world-model planning with a simple, implementable combination of randomized grouped-attention training and inference-time token subsampling.

Experiments cover six simulated environments and demonstrate useful operating points. At 50% dropout, Pointmaze success increases from 98.3% to 100% while planning time falls by 49.5%; Wall success increases from 85% to 95% with a 32.9% time reduction.

Includes comparisons with several token-selection strategies, grouped-attention ablations, representation probing, and noise-robustness experiments. These provide useful evidence beyond the main performance tables.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental relative to DINO-WM and existing patch-dropout methods. The grouped-attention ablation does not compare against straightforward random-subset training or conventional PatchDropout, leaving the value of the specific training innovation insufficiently established.

The main planning results lack confidence intervals and repeated-training-seed results, with only 20–60 evaluation episodes per environment. Claims of improved performance or no significant advantage for alternative selectors are therefore inadequately supported; averaging success across dropout ratios also obscures individual trade-offs.

The claim that performance generally remains stable through 50% dropout is too broad. PushT falls from 75% to 56.7% at 40% dropout, and Granular falls from 75% to 60% at 50%. Block Pushing success remains only 12–28%, limiting evidence for reliable, precise manipulation.

The efficiency evaluation lacks comparisons at matched planning-time budgets, such as reducing CEM candidates or iterations, and lacks a runtime breakdown separating encoding, dynamics prediction, and other overhead. Reported planning times remain 53–208 seconds per iteration at 50% dropout, which does not substantiate claims about real-time control.

Comparisons with sophisticated compression methods are not conclusive. LTRP and STAR use ImageNet-derived importance, while ATC introduces pooled representations and Hungarian matching without a clearly documented matching training adaptation. These results evaluate particular adaptations rather than establish the general superiority of random selection.

The explanatory analyses overreach their evidence. Linear-kernel nHSIC measures dependence rather than mutual information and cannot generally certify independence. The Granular probe predicts only coordinate means and standard deviations, not detailed state. An absence of visible structure in UMAP plots does not justify modeling dropout errors as input-independent, zero-mean Gaussian noise, so the synthetic-noise experiment does not validate robustness to actual structured prediction errors.

Reproducibility and technical reporting need improvement: success thresholds and exact timing conditions are unspecified, Appendix A.2 conflicts with task-specific training epochs and MPC limits elsewhere, and Section 3.2 incorrectly describes token-dependent computation as exponential. Together with the missing baseline controls and statistical evidence, these issues leave the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant bottleneck in visual world-model planning with a simple, practical method: randomized grouped-attention training followed by token subsampling during imagined rollouts.

Experiments cover six simulated environments and demonstrate useful operating points. At 50% dropout, Pointmaze achieves 100% versus 98.3% success while reducing planning time from 184 to 93 seconds; Wall achieves 95% versus 85% with a reduction from 79 to 53 seconds.

The evaluation includes multiple token-selection strategies, a fixed-mask comparison, grouped-attention ablations, and representation probes. These provide evidence that random subsets can support planning and that training for sparse inputs is beneficial.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental relative to DINO-WM and existing token-dropout methods. The grouped-attention strategy is plausible, but comparison against conventional random-token-dropout training is missing, leaving its specific advantage insufficiently established.

The central performance-preservation claim is stronger than the results support. PushT success drops from 75% to 56.7% at 40% dropout, and Granular drops from 75% to 60% at 50%. Block Pushing remains weak throughout, at 12–28% success. A reliable procedure for choosing the dropout ratio without tuning on evaluation outcomes is not provided.

Main planning results use only 20–60 episodes per setting and provide no confidence intervals or variability across independently trained models. Several claimed improvements correspond to only a few successful episodes. Averaging across dropout ratios in Table 3 also obscures the relevant accuracy–latency trade-offs and does not establish statistical equivalence between selection methods.

Efficiency comparisons do not include equal-wall-clock-budget planning baselines, such as full-token planning with fewer CEM candidates or optimization iterations. Reported latency remains tens to hundreds of seconds per MPC iteration, so real-time deployment is not demonstrated. Timing hardware allocation and component-level costs are insufficiently specified.

The mechanistic analysis overstates its conclusions. Normalized HSIC measures kernel dependence, not mutual information or retained task-relevant information. The Granular probe predicts only particle-coordinate means and standard deviations, which cannot establish preservation of detailed geometry. Absence of visible structure in a UMAP plot of error magnitudes does not justify modeling prediction errors as input-independent, zero-mean Gaussian noise.

The token-selection comparisons have unresolved fairness limitations. Several importance estimators are derived from ImageNet or image-reconstruction objectives rather than planning. The clustering baseline changes token distributions and spatial correspondence, but matched training for this representation is not clearly established. Its poor performance therefore does not isolate an inherent disadvantage of merging.

Reproducibility and technical precision need improvement. Appendix training epochs and maximum MPC iterations conflict with other descriptions; success criteria and evaluation splits are insufficiently explicit. Section 3.2 incorrectly describes token-count scaling as exponential, whereas standard self-attention scales quadratically. These issues, together with the evaluation gaps, leave the paper below the acceptance threshold despite its useful empirical direction.

Includes comparisons with multiple token-selection strategies, grouped-attention ablations, representation probing, and noise-sensitivity experiments. The grouped-attention results provide positive evidence that training for sparse inputs improves robustness.
weaknesses: The methodological advance over DINO-WM and existing patch-dropout techniques is incremental, and the distinctive grouped-attention design is not compared against ordinary random-token-dropout training. This missing baseline prevents establishing whether the proposed training mechanism is necessary.

The central performance-preservation claim lacks adequate statistical support. Main planning results use only 20–60 episodes per environment, without confidence intervals or reported variability across independently trained models. Degradation is also substantial at some moderate dropout rates: PushT falls from 75.0% to 56.7% at 40% dropout, and Granular from 75.0% to 60.0% at 50%.

Efficiency evaluation does not establish competitiveness at a fixed computational budget. There are no comparisons against full-token planning with fewer CEM candidates or iterations, or a smaller world model. Reported times remain 53–208 seconds per planning iteration at 50% dropout, so real-time control is not demonstrated; timing scope, inference hardware allocation, and runtime variability need clarification.

The explanatory analysis overstates its conclusions. An absence of visible structure in a UMAP plot does not justify modeling rollout errors as input-independent, zero-mean Gaussian noise; synthetic-noise robustness therefore does not establish robustness to actual structured model errors.

Comparisons do not conclusively establish that sophisticated token reduction offers no advantage. Table 3 aggregates success across dropout rates without uncertainty or clearly specified aggregation, and the clustering adaptation introduces distribution shift and Hungarian-matching overhead. It is unclear whether competing representations receive appropriately matched training.

Reproducibility and presentation need improvement: Appendix A.2 gives training epochs and MPC limits that conflict with dataset-specific settings elsewhere, task-success thresholds are insufficiently specified, and Section 3.2 incorrectly describes token-dependent computational scaling as exponential. Overall, the promising practical results do not yet provide sufficiently controlled evidence for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in visual world-model planning with a simple, implementable approach: randomized grouped-attention training followed by sparse token rollouts.

The evaluation is broad, covering navigation, rigid and deformable object manipulation, LIBERO-10, Meta-World, and two physical robot tasks. Additional experiments test alternative visual encoders and gradient-based planning.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial. At 50% token dropout, average planning time decreases by 40.5% across four environments, while average success across the six basic benchmarks remains approximately unchanged. The component-level profiling supports the proposed computational explanation.

The paper includes useful comparisons against several token-selection strategies and ablations supporting grouped-attention training. Quantitative blind-spot measurements provide evidence beyond illustrative examples.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest relative to existing token dropout and DINO-WM. The paper does not compare grouped-attention training against straightforward random-token-dropout training, leaving unclear whether its main training contribution is necessary or preferable. Comparisons against reducing candidate counts or optimization steps at matched runtime would also strengthen the efficiency claim.

The main success-rate comparisons lack confidence intervals and clearly reported independent training runs. Real-world results use only ten trials per task, so the claimed improvements over VLA-only correspond to two additional successes for PickPlace and one for Drawer. LIBERO's improvement from 29% to 33% over 100 trials is likewise weak evidence of a reliable gain.

The real-world generalization description is inconsistent: Section 4.3 states that both tasks use unseen initial block locations, whereas Appendix A.1 explicitly says Drawer is evaluated at positions included in training. This materially weakens the claimed held-out evaluation.

Performance preservation is overstated. At 50% dropout, PushT decreases from 75% to 70% and Granular from 75% to 60%; at 40% dropout, PushT falls to 56.7%. Similar aggregate averages conceal meaningful task-specific losses, and statistical equivalence is not established.

The real-time deployment claim needs clearer measurements. Basic MPC still requires tens to hundreds of seconds per reported iteration. Robot results report episode-level times with asynchronous execution, rather than separating inference latency, physical execution, and waiting time or demonstrating that planning consistently meets control deadlines.

The comparisons and analyses do not fully establish a fundamental advantage of random selection. Several competing selectors use image-based importance criteria, and clustering is evaluated with the same world model despite changing token semantics. State probing predicts only particle-coordinate means and standard deviations, while the Gaussian-error model is motivated by visual inspection of UMAP plots; neither establishes preservation of all planning-relevant information or the actual structure of rollout errors.

Important implementation details remain unclear, including the precise mask-resampling schedule and how proprioceptive distance enters the planning objective. The latter is consequential because the vision-only Wall experiment changes performance substantially, yet the main objective specifies only visual-feature distance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in visual world-model planning with a simple, plausible approach: randomized grouped-attention training followed by sparse token rollouts.

The efficiency gains are substantial and supported by component-level profiling. At 50% dropout, average planning time decreases by 40.5% across four environments, while average success across six environments remains approximately unchanged.

Evaluation is broad, covering navigation, manipulation, deformable objects, LIBERO, Meta-World, and two physical-robot tasks. Additional experiments examine alternative encoders, gradient-based planning, and adaptive sparsity.

Comparisons include several token-selection strategies, and grouped-attention ablations support the training mechanism. The quantitative blind-spot analysis provides useful evidence beyond illustrative examples.
weaknesses: The methodological advance over existing patch dropout and DINO-WM is modest, and its necessity is incompletely established. Grouped attention is compared with full-attention training, but not ordinary random-token-dropout training or variable-sparsity training, leaving the benefit of the specific proposed mechanism unclear.

The main control results lack uncertainty estimates and repeated-training-seed reporting. Physical experiments use only 10 trials per task: the reported improvements correspond to two additional PickPlace successes and one additional Drawer success. LIBERO improves from 29% to 33% over 100 trials. These results do not establish reliable improvements or equivalence to full-token planning.

There is a material inconsistency in the real-world generalization claim. Section 4.3 states that both tasks use initial block locations unseen during training, whereas Appendix A.1 states that Drawer evaluation uses two training locations.

Efficiency comparisons do not establish the best performance attainable at a fixed compute budget. Important alternatives include full-token planning with fewer candidates or CEM iterations and smaller world models. The appendix's CEM-step ablation does not provide a matched-latency comparison.

Several explanations exceed the evidence. Granular probing predicts only aggregate particle-position statistics, which cannot establish preservation of fine-grained planning information. Lack of visible structure in a UMAP plot does not justify modeling prediction errors as independent zero-mean Gaussian noise. Blind-spot measurements support a plausible mechanism but do not prove that random subsets almost certainly retain sufficient information.

The real-time claim needs clearer timing evidence. CEM planning still takes tens to hundreds of seconds per iteration; robotic results report episode-level timings with asynchronous execution, without a clear breakdown of decision latency and control deadlines. Overall, the useful speedups and extensive experiments place the paper near the threshold, but missing controls, statistical uncertainty, and overstated claims leave it below acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in visual world-model planning with a simple, useful approach: randomized grouped-attention training enables inference using subsets of spatial tokens without requiring a learned selector.

The central efficiency result has concrete support. At 50% dropout, average success across six environments is 69.7% versus 69.8% for full tokens, while average planning time across four environments decreases by 40.5%. Component-level profiling supports the proposed source of acceleration.

Evaluation is unusually broad for a simple method, covering CEM, gradient-based planning, policy-guided planning, multiple visual encoders, manipulation benchmarks, and two physical robot tasks. Meta-World retains 47.73% success versus 48.80% with full tokens while reducing reported planning time from 3.63 to 2.37 seconds per episode.

Comparisons include several token-selection families, and the grouped-attention ablation provides evidence that training adaptation matters. The blind-spot analysis offers a useful, experimentally motivated explanation for why static importance scores can underperform random selection.
weaknesses: Performance-preservation claims need better statistical support. Most control results lack confidence intervals or variation across independently trained models, and individual tasks show meaningful declines: at 50% dropout, Granular falls from 75% to 60% and PushT from 75% to 70%. Only 10 trials per physical task make the reported gains over VLA-only equivalent to one or two additional successes.

The real-world generalization description is inconsistent. Section 4.3 says both tasks use unseen initial block locations, whereas Appendix A.1 explicitly evaluates Drawer at training locations. Fixed receptacle poses and very few test locations also limit the demonstrated deployment generality.

The novelty is primarily an effective application and combination of existing token-dropout ideas. Comparing grouped attention with ordinary random token-dropout training would better establish its distinct contribution. Equal-latency comparisons against full-token planning with fewer candidates or optimization steps are also missing, leaving the practical compute-allocation advantage incompletely established.

Several explanatory claims exceed the evidence. Visual inspection of a UMAP projection does not justify treating prediction errors as input-independent, zero-mean Gaussian noise. Likewise, dependence measures and probing particle-position means and variances do not establish preservation of all information needed for control. The blind-spot measurements support an association, but do not fully establish the claimed causal explanation.

Timing and implementation reporting need clarification. CEM planning still takes tens to hundreds of seconds per iteration, so real-time claims should be restricted to the asynchronous policy-guided setting. The precise timing boundaries, device allocation, and contribution of proprioceptive distance to the planning objective are insufficiently specified. The token-selector comparison also averages across dropout levels, obscuring individual accuracy–latency trade-offs.
